archetype.name: Better Than Its Record (5-on-5 driven)
archetype.definition: Columbus is out-chancing teams at even strength but losing games on its penalty kill and in its crease, so the 2-3-0 start undersells how it actually plays.

report.headline: Good 5-on-5 process, sunk by a leaky penalty kill and below-average goaltending
report.take:
Columbus has spent two seasons climbing out of a rebuild. It went from 30th on the site in 2022-23 to 21st and then 18th, and last year it finally broke even on goals with a 0.52 xGF % and a goaltending group that saved 7.8 goals above expected. The 2-3-0 start and a 27th-place site rank look like a step back. The underlying play doesn't. At 5-on-5 this team is winning the chance battle at a 0.539 xGF % (12th) and splitting shot attempts down the middle. Nearly every regular forward is above 0.52 individually, led by Adam Fantilli at 0.607.

The damage is concentrated in two places. The penalty kill is at 0.611, 29th in the league, and the goalies are 4.4 goals below expected, also 29th. Jet Greaves has a 0.874 save % over his three starts and Cam Talbot carries a 4.43 GAA. That is how a team that controls play ends up 29th in goals against per game, with the 7-3 loss to Florida as the loudest example. PDO is 100.9, so 5-on-5 bounces aren't the culprit. The goals are getting through on the kill and on stops an average goalie would make.

The roster has a clear shape. Zach Werenski logs 28.91 minutes a night at a 0.583 xGF %, and Damon Severson has been even better when available (0.637 in three games). Below them it falls apart. Erik Gudbranson (0.388) and Carson Soucy (0.431) get caved in, and both sit near the bottom of the defense tab. That is the D+ blueline grade in a nutshell. Up front, scoring is spread rather than starred. Cole Sillinger and Kent Johnson have three goals each, Charlie Coyle has five assists, and Conor Garland has yet to register a point. The C- forward grade reflects depth without a true driver.

Five games is a tiny sample, and the parts that are hurting most are the noisiest ones: penalty-kill percentage and goalie GSAx swing wildly over a handful of games. The exception is the PK. It sat in the 0.75-0.79 range for each of the last five seasons, so it is a long-running weakness rather than a fluke. Expect the goaltending to drift back toward average and the kill to improve, though not to good. If the 5-on-5 edge holds, this is roughly the .500-ish team of last season rather than a bottom-five club.

strengths.title: Winning the chance battle at even strength
strengths.body: A 0.539 xGF % ranks 12th and continues last season's 0.52. That marked the first time in this window that Columbus out-chanced opponents, so the improvement looks structural. It is broad-based, with Fantilli, Knies and Coyle all well above 0.55. This is the most stable part of the profile and the reason to expect better results.

strengths.title: Werenski anchoring heavy minutes
strengths.body: Werenski plays nearly 29 minutes a game and is still on the right side of the chances, with a +5 and four assists. Severson has matched that impact in limited games. As long as those two drive the top pairing, the team's even-strength foundation holds.

strengths.title: Scoring spread across the lineup
strengths.body: Columbus is getting goals from the middle of the lineup, with Sillinger and Johnson leading the way, rather than leaning on one star. The forwards have combined for 13 goals, and the offense sits a respectable 17th. That depth lowers the risk of a scoring drought, though it also caps the ceiling.

concerns.title: A penalty kill bleeding goals
concerns.body: A 0.611 PK % ranks 29th and goes a long way toward explaining a 29th-ranked defense despite good 5-on-5 numbers. The rate itself is a small-sample extreme. The underlying problem isn't new, though: the kill finished between 0.75 and 0.79 in each of the last five seasons. Expect improvement toward that old level, not toward league average.

concerns.title: Goaltending well below expected
concerns.body: The tandem is 4.4 goals below expected, 29th, after being a strength last season. Greaves' 0.874 save % and Talbot's -2.1 GSAx in two starts both point the same way, and the group grades D-. Some of this is five-game noise, but the team has no margin if neither goalie stabilizes.

concerns.title: Bottom pair and wingers against
concerns.body: Gudbranson and Soucy are getting badly out-chanced. Opposing wingers are scoring well above their norms against Columbus, the worst mark in the league by that measure. The third pair is where opponents are generating, and it won't fix itself without lineup changes.

trend.note: Columbus has alternated wins and losses all month without a streak longer than two, beating Buffalo and Pittsburgh at home and dropping the other three. The 7-3 loss to Florida is the low point.

weekAhead.headline: Three top-half opponents, including a back-to-back, test the leaky kill
weekAhead.body:
The week opens with the Rangers at home, then a back-to-back in Minnesota, then Toronto back in Columbus. The Rangers sit 3rd on the site, but their record rides a 105.4 PDO and the league's best goaltending. Their shot share (0.46 CF %, 25th) is worse than Columbus's. If the Jackets keep pushing play, the game is more winnable than the standings suggest. Even so, out-chancing a team whose goalies lead the league in GSAx is no guarantee of goals.

Minnesota on the second night is the danger spot. The Wild's power play is the best in the league at 0.368, and Columbus's kill is 29th, so discipline decides that one. Toronto closes the week as the softest opponent on paper by process: a 0.411 xGF % (28th) and a D blueline. Its kill is perfect-ish at 0.958, though, so Columbus has to win at 5-on-5. Taking two of three would be a good week. One win is the realistic baseline.

keyMatchups.title: Columbus PK vs Wild power play
keyMatchups.body: Minnesota converts 0.368 of its chances, first in the league, against a Columbus kill at 0.611. Taking penalties on the second half of a back-to-back is how this game gets away. Winning the special-teams minutes even narrowly would be a real step.

keyMatchups.title: Out-chancing a hot Rangers team
keyMatchups.body: New York is getting outshot at 5-on-5 but riding a 105.4 PDO and league-best goaltending. Columbus's 0.539 xGF % gives it the puck-control edge. The question is whether it can solve goaltenders playing well above expected.

keyMatchups.title: Toronto's weak 5-on-5 game
keyMatchups.body: The Leafs rank 28th in xGF % with a D-graded blueline, which plays directly into Columbus's strength. Their kill is at 0.958, so the Jackets' 19th-ranked power play likely won't bail them out. Even-strength chances have to turn into goals.

weekAhead.watch: Whether Columbus can stay out of the box in Minnesota and keep the league's top power play from deciding the back-to-back.

restOfSeason.body:
The most sustainable piece is the 5-on-5 chance share, a continuation of last season's gains. The least sustainable pieces are the ones dragging the record down: a 0.611 kill and goalies 4.4 goals below expected rarely persist at those depths over a full season. Regression should work in Columbus's favor and pull goals against down from 4.2 a game toward the low threes. The kill's long history in the 0.75-0.79 range says it will stay a weakness, not become a strength.

The ceiling is limited by a thin bottom pair and a forward group without a dominant scorer. The floor is supported by Werenski and broad even-strength play. That points to a team hovering around .500 and fighting for a wild-card spot rather than living at 27th. It most resembles last season's 40-win outcome, with the goaltending deciding which side of the bubble it lands on.
swingFactors: Penalty-kill improvement toward its historical level
Upgrading or sheltering the Gudbranson-Soucy pair

confidence.note: Five games: special teams and goalie numbers are especially noisy.
